140 - Avatar and Philosophy - Learning t: Avatar: The Last Airbender is a beloved Nickelodeon animated series (2005-2008) about Aang, a reluctant twelve-year-old savior who must master the four elements to end a century of imperial war. Its mix of Asian and Indigenous traditions, morally complicated villains, and a hero who refuses to kill gives it unusual depth for a children's show. This book asks what the series teaches about oneness, interdependence, chosen-one tropes, martial ethics, and whether nations themselves are illusions.
141 - Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Phi: Avatar: The Last Airbender, Nickelodeon's acclaimed animated epic (2005-2008), follows Aang and his friends as they resist the Fire Nation's conquest in a world where people bend the four elements. The show's writers deliberately tested their characters' beliefs against their humanity, and its themes of genocide, imperialism, and the 'illusion of separation' invite serious thought. Essays here explore identity, disability, trust, and what a Chosen One story becomes when saving the world is a team effort.
142 - The Avengers and Philosophy - Eart: The Avengers are Marvel Comics' flagship superhero team, famous since 1963 for pairing gods, soldiers, and geniuses with endless interpersonal drama. Because the team keeps quarreling over principle as much as villainy, it is rich material for philosophy. Chapters ask whether Iron Man, Captain America, and Thor embody utilitarian, deontologist, and virtue ethics; whether reformed villains deserve forgiveness; who counts as the real Captain America; and whether an android can truly love.
143 - Batman and Philosophy - The Dark K: Batman, DC Comics' brooding vigilante, has fought Gotham's rogues gallery since 1939, and no hero's code invites harder questions. The essays here ask why Batman will not simply kill the Joker, whether it was right to recruit children as Robin, if a madman like the Joker can be held responsible at all, and whether Batman's existence exposes the failure of the state itself. His obsession, hatred, and discipline make him a philosophical case study, not just a hero.
144 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosoph: Battlestar Galactica was the Syfy channel's acclaimed reimagining (2004-2009) of a 1978 space opera: the last remnants of humanity flee genocidal Cylons, machines that now look and feel human. The show was famous for taking on war, torture, abortion, and insurgency without flinching. Its questions run deep: if your memories and body betray you, who are you; can humans and their destroyers ever become one people; and what does our own history repeat when 'all of this has happened before'?
145 - The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy: The Big Bang Theory was one of American television's most popular sitcoms (CBS, 2007-2019), following four brilliant but socially awkward scientists and the neighbor who humanizes them. Its running joke, that genius is no substitute for wisdom, is genuinely philosophical territory. Chapters weigh Sheldon's life of pure thought against Aristotle's ideal of flourishing, test the roommate agreement against Hobbes, probe the ethics of laughing at Sheldon's autistic-coded traits, and ask whether the gang's friendships are real at all.
146 - The Big Lebowski and Philosophy -: The Big Lebowski is the Coen brothers' 1998 cult comedy about the Dude, an unemployed Los Angeles slacker mistaken for a millionaire and drawn into a kidnapping plot over a soiled rug. A box-office flop that became a way of life for its fans, it is quietly serious about how to live. Essays set the Dude's pacifist 'abiding' against Aristotle, Epicurus, and nihilism, asking whether his leisure is wisdom or waste, and what his friendships are really worth.
147 - Bioshock and Philosophy - Irration: BioShock is a landmark video game series (2007 onward) set in failed utopias: the underwater city of Rapture, built on Ayn Rand-style objectivism, and the flying city of Columbia, built on American exceptionalism. Famous for its 'would you kindly' twist, which revealed the player's own choices were scripted, it turns games into philosophy. Chapters examine free will, whether the game fairly critiques Rand, Elizabeth's feminist liberation, and what ghosts and plasmids say about minds and bodies.
148 - Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark: Black Mirror is Charlie Brooker's acclaimed British anthology series (2011 onward) of standalone near-future dramas about technology and its discontents, from social-media ratings to digital resurrection of the dead. Each episode works like a philosophical thought experiment rather than a simple gadget warning. Essays here ask whether coercion for the greater good is ever justified, what total transparency does to trust, whether a copy of your dead lover is your lover, and what justice really means when punishment becomes entertainment.
149 - Black Panther and Philosophy - Wha: Black Panther (2018) made Marvel Comics' first Black superhero, created in 1966, into a cultural phenomenon: T'Challa, king of Wakanda, a secretly ultra-advanced African nation, torn between isolation and the world's oppressed. The film became a rare mainstream arena for debates about colonialism, reparations, and Afrofuturism. Chapters pit T'Challa's liberal internationalism against Killmonger's Pan-Africanism, weigh Wakanda's debts to the diaspora, and ask what African philosophy itself would have Wakanda offer the world.
